title: Counsel the doubtful
tomorrow: what did a man stuck on his reading need most?

lines: SIDE BY SIDE, IN THE DARK.
cards: Some of the best talks happen side by side. In a car after dark. On a walk around the block.
Nobody has to look anybody in the eye, so the hard thing finally gets said. Luke tells of two disciples walking away from Jerusalem, talking over everything that's happened. Their teacher is dead.

Then, in the Douay-Rheims, "Jesus himself also drawing near, went with them." They don't know him. And before one word of explanation, he does two things: he falls into step, and he asks what they're talking about.

teach.b: Listen to the order on the road to Emmaus. First the footsteps; he matches their pace.
Then the question. Then he lets them talk. They pour it out: a prophet mighty in deed and word, crucified, and now some women saying the tomb is empty.
And the sentence that holds it all: we had hoped. Only then does he speak. Yes, he calls them slow of heart, and then he opens the Scriptures to them along the road.
They know him when he breaks bread at their table, and afterward they say their hearts burned while he talked with them on the way. On the way: the whole conversation happened walking.

The traditional list of spiritual works of mercy calls this counseling the doubtful. It's less about winning an argument than keeping someone company on a hard road. And the Gospels don't treat doubt as a crime.
In Mark, a father brings his suffering son and says, "I do believe, Lord: help my unbelief." Belief and unbelief in one breath, and Jesus heals the boy.
So the work starts with walking and listening long enough to hear the we had hoped. A friend's late text saying she isn't sure anymore. A kid's hard question at bedtime.
The counselor doesn't need every answer first. On that road, the questions came first.

how: Catholics offer this work through spiritual direction, through parish and campus ministers who meet with people in doubt, and in ordinary friendship, often simply by listening.

o: send a doubter to go see a priest
win an argument against a skeptic
walk with and listen to someone unsure

games.q: on the road — tap the pairs.
p: fell into step and asked a question

s: in the Gospels, doubt is treated as a crime
a father says help my unbelief, and Jesus heals his son.
the two disciples knew Jesus as soon as he joined them
they knew him only when he broke bread at their table.
the stranger listened before he explained the Scriptures
he asked, let them say we had hoped, and only then spoke.

games.q: your cousin texts at 1 a.m.: i don't think i believe any of it anymore. you have a stack of good arguments ready. what does the Emmaus road do first?
o: ask what's been happening, and let him talk it all out.
send your strongest argument now, while he's still awake.
tell him everyone doubts sometimes and it'll pass soon.
games.why: the stranger fell into step and asked a question before he explained anything. they said we had hoped, and only then did he speak.

practice: Stand up and walk slowly wherever you are: a hallway, a room, a sidewalk. Feel each step land, and match your pace to someone in your mind who is carrying a question right now, the way the stranger matched theirs.
If you pray, you can walk the sit as a prayer for them; if not, just keep them company, step by step.

wordCard.voice: Counsel the doubtful. Walk beside someone who isn't sure, listen first, and speak when it helps.

orig.note: Greek: he was walking along with them. Luke's word for the stranger on the road (24:15).

carryVoice: Your line: walk with doubt. On the road to Emmaus, the questions came before the answers. Go gently.
